## Overview

A TWAS Z-score (see the
[TWAS Z-score + MR vignette](twas-zscore.html)) asks whether a gene's
predicted expression associates with the trait. It asks that question one
gene at a time, so a gene can score highly purely because it sits near a
strong GWAS signal that is really driven by a nearby variant.

`ctwasPipeline()` runs
[cTWAS](https://github.com/xinhe-lab/multigroup_ctwas), which fine-maps
**genes and SNPs jointly within each LD block**. A gene's posterior
inclusion probability is therefore conditioned on the SNP signal beside it,
which is what separates a gene that carries the association from one that
merely neighbours it.

Inputs:

| Argument | What it is |
|---|---|
| `gwasSumStats` | one `GwasSumStats` whose elements are LD blocks |
| `twasWeights` | per-gene `TwasWeights` / `QtlFineMappingResult` |
| `twasZ` | optional pre-computed per-gene Z from `causalInferencePipeline()` |
| `fineMappingResult` | optional `QtlFineMappingResult` for the rescues |

```{r load-packages}
library(pecotmr)
```

## The LD block convention

`gwasSumStats` is **one** `GwasSumStats` object whose elements are LD
blocks, keyed by its `blockId` column — not a list of per-block objects.
Build it with `loadGwasSumStatsFromManifest(..., which = <blocks>)` and
pass it through `summaryStatsQc()`.

A single-block input is rejected: cTWAS estimates its group priors by EM
across regions, and one region gives it nothing to average over.

```{r bundled}
ldStem <- file.path(
    system.file("extdata", "ld_reference", "chr22", package = "pecotmr"),
    "protocol_example.LD.chr22"
)
gwasTsv <- system.file(
    "extdata",
    "manifests",
    "protocol_example.twas.gwas_sumstats.chr22.tsv.gz",
    package = "pecotmr"
)

blocks <- GenomicRanges::GRanges(
    "chr22",
    IRanges::IRanges(c(10000000, 15000001), c(15000000, 19000000)),
    blockId = c("chr22_1", "chr22_2")
)

gwasSumStats <- loadGwasSumStatsFromManifest(
    manifest = data.frame(study = "gwas1", sumStatsPath = gwasTsv),
    genome = "hg38",
    ldReference = ldStem,
    which = blocks
)
gwasByRegion <- summaryStatsQc(
    gwasSumStats,
    panelFilterParam = PanelFilterParam(mafCutoff = 0.0025)
)

data(ctwasWeightsExample)
```

## Running the pipeline

```{r ctwas-run}
res <- ctwasPipeline(
    gwasSumStats = gwasByRegion,
    twasWeights = list(ctwasWeightsExample),
    method = "susie",
    ctwasPriorParam = CtwasPriorParam(
        thin = 1,
        niterPrefit = 3,
        niter = 10,
        fallbackToPrefit = TRUE
    ),
    methodArgs = CtwasOptions(
        regionData = CtwasRegionDataOptions(min_group_size = 1),
        estParam = CtwasEstParamOptions(
            min_group_size = 1,
            min_p_single_effect = 0
        ),
        screen = CtwasScreenOptions(min_nonSNP_PIP = 0)
    )
)
res
```

The settings above are sized for a toy dataset and are **not** defaults you
should carry into a real analysis:

- `thin = 1` keeps every SNP (production runs thin to `0.1`).
- `niterPrefit` / `niter` are cut to keep the vignette fast.
- `min_nonSNP_PIP = 0` disables region screening. The bundled GWAS has no
    genome-wide-significant signal, so the default (`0.5`) selects no region at
    all and the result comes back empty. On real data, leave it alone.
- `fallbackToPrefit = TRUE` recovers from the accurate-EM step returning
    `NaN` on underpowered data by keeping the prefit estimates.

## Where genes come from

`twasWeights` accepts two shapes:

- a **flat** `TwasWeights` or `QtlFineMappingResult` (or a homogeneous list
    of them), each gene read with the LD block holding most of its weight. A
    gene's `traitPos`, if it has one, only gives its coordinates in the
    results.
- a **pre-bucketed named list** keyed by `region_id`, used as-is, each gene in
    one block.

Blocks with no gene weights do not feed the group priors by default: cTWAS
skips regions with fewer genes than its `min_gene`, 1. To let their SNP-level
signal in, set `min_gene = 0` in `CtwasEstParamOptions()`.

A gene's weights are used whole, whichever blocks they fall in; see
[Boundary genes](#boundary-genes).

A run estimates one prior per group, and a group is a study, context and
molecular type, each estimated from its own genes. So the contexts need not
hold the same genes, and two studies with one context name stay apart. The type
is the `dataType` the data records, through `QtlDataset(dataType = )` or
`QtlSumStats(dataType = )`, which the pipelines carry onto the weights; where
none is recorded, a gene's type is `"QTL"`. Groups share one prior variance by
default (`varStructure = "shared_nonSNP"`), since a group with few causal genes
has little to estimate its own from, and `"shared_type"` pools them within each
molecular type instead.

cTWAS leaves a group with fewer genes than `min_group_size` (100 by default) out
of the fit, and `estCtwasGroupPriors()` warns when it does. To keep it, lower
`min_group_size` in both `CtwasRegionDataOptions()` and
`CtwasEstParamOptions()`: the second stops on a group under its own limit.

## Trimming each gene's variants

Weight matrices from a permissive QTL model can be large, and cTWAS's cost
scales with them. Four arguments trim each gene before cTWAS sees it:

| Argument | Effect |
|---|---|
| `weightCutoff` | drop variants with `abs(weight)` below the cutoff |
| `maxVariants` | cap variants per gene |
| `csMinCor` | keep variants in a credible set with purity at least this |
| `pipRescue` | keep variants with PIP above this |

`csMinCor` and `pipRescue` mark variants as must-keep, so they survive
the `maxVariants` cap. Both need a `fineMappingResult`; without one they
are no-ops and the cap falls back to ordering by `abs(weight)`. With one,
`fineMappingMethod` names which of its fine-mapping methods they read: a
weight's own method, such as an ensemble, names no fine-mapping fit.

```{r ctwas-filters, eval=FALSE}
ctwasPipeline(
    gwasSumStats = gwasByRegion,
    twasWeights = list(ctwasWeightsExample),
    method = "susie",
    fineMappingResult = fmr,
    fineMappingMethod = "susie",
    variantPruningParam = VariantPruningParam(
        weightCutoff = 1e-4,
        maxVariants = 1000,
        csMinCor = 0.8,
        pipRescue = 0.1
    )
)
```

## Reading the result

`ctwasPipeline()` returns a `CtwasResult`: one row per
`(gwasStudy, study, context, method)` run and cTWAS region, the way a
`GwasFineMappingResult` holds a genome-wide fit as one row per LD block.

```{r ctwas-identity}
methodNames(res)
studyName(res)
contexts(res)
```

The per-gene posteriors live in `ctwasPosteriors()`:

```{r ctwas-finemap}
fm <- ctwasPosteriors(res)
as.data.frame(fm)[, c(
    "molecular_id",
    "context",
    "region_id",
    "z",
    "susie_pip",
    "cs"
)]
```

`susie_pip` is the quantity cTWAS exists to produce: the probability the
gene is causal given the SNPs it competes with. Here it is low (the toy GWAS
has no real signal) and `cs` is `NA` because the gene falls in no credible
set.

`susieAlpha()` returns the per-single-effect alpha matrix behind those
PIPs. The group priors are the run's one genome-wide estimate: the EM step
fits them across every region, and each region is then fine-mapped under
them. `ctwasGroupPriors()` lists them once per run, one row per group. A group
is named `{study}_{context}_{type}`, with the three as columns of their own,
since those underscores cannot be split back. Beside its size, prior inclusion
probability and prior effect variance are cTWAS's summary of them: each gene
group's enrichment over the SNP group, and the heritability each group explains:

```{r ctwas-param}
ctwasGroupPriors(res)
```

A gene modelled through several molecular traits or contexts has one PIP for
each. `ctwasCombinedPips()` gives the probability that it is causal through any
of them. Pass a `mapping` from molecular ids to gene names when the ids of a
gene's traits differ, as an expression and a splicing trait's do:

```{r ctwas-combined}
ctwasCombinedPips(res)
```

The rest of the EM output, iteration traces and convergence flag included,
sits in the `groupPriors` column, the same on every region of the run:

```{r ctwas-em}
res$groupPriors[[1]]$converged
```

By default the context-agnostic SNP background is dropped from the result,
since it is the null the genes are being scored against rather than a
finding. Pass `keepSnps = TRUE` to retain it as extra rows, one per region
(`study = context = "SNP"`), which makes the full cTWAS output
reconstructable.

## The four chainable steps

`ctwasPipeline()` is a wrapper over four steps. Call them directly when you
want to inspect an intermediate payload, override the estimated priors, or
re-enter the chain without recomputing what came before.

```{r ctwas-granular}
inputs <- assembleCtwasInputs(
    gwasSumStats = gwasByRegion,
    twasWeights = list(ctwasWeightsExample),
    method = "susie"
)
est <- estCtwasGroupPriors(
    inputs,
    ctwasPriorParam = CtwasPriorParam(
        thin = 1,
        niterPrefit = 3,
        niter = 10,
        fallbackToPrefit = TRUE
    ),
    methodArgs = CtwasOptions(
        regionData = CtwasRegionDataOptions(min_group_size = 1),
        estParam = CtwasEstParamOptions(
            min_group_size = 1,
            min_p_single_effect = 0
        )
    )
)
screened <- screenCtwasRegions(
    est,
    methodArgs = CtwasOptions(
        screen = CtwasScreenOptions(min_nonSNP_PIP = 0)
    )
)
finemapped <- finemapCtwasRegions(screened)
nrow(finemapped$finemap_res)
```

`finemap_res` here has more rows than `ctwasPosteriors(res)` above: it still
carries the SNP rows. `asCtwasResult()` is the step that structures the
payload and drops them.

```{r ctwas-as-result}
length(ctwasPosteriors(asCtwasResult(finemapped)))
length(ctwasPosteriors(asCtwasResult(finemapped, keepSnps = TRUE)))
```

Each step's payload is also bundled, so you can enter anywhere:

```{r ctwas-bundled-payloads, eval=FALSE}
data(ctwasInputsExample) # after assembleCtwasInputs
data(ctwasEstExample) # after estCtwasGroupPriors
data(ctwasFinemapExample) # after finemapCtwasRegions
```

The most common reason to use the granular path is to override the priors.
`estCtwasGroupPriors()`'s accurate-EM step can diverge on underpowered data;
`fallbackToPrefit = TRUE` handles that automatically, but taking the steps
apart lets you substitute priors of your own into `screenCtwasRegions()`.

## Boundary genes

A gene whose weights cross an LD block boundary is modelled as cTWAS models it.
Its z-score reads all its weights, and it is fine-mapped in the block holding
the largest share of its absolute weights, with the part of its weights in that
block. That first pass can call a gene whose real signal is a variant across the
boundary, since the block it is fine-mapped in has no LD to explain the signal
by. So `ctwasPipeline()` merges the regions of a high-PIP boundary gene and
fine-maps them again, as cTWAS's own post-processing does. In simulations
through `ctwasPipeline()` on real LD, a non-causal gene reading a causal variant
across the boundary reached a PIP above 0.5 in up to 93% of regions after the
first pass and in up to 16% after merging, while a causal boundary gene reached
it in at least 96% either way.

`BoundaryMergeParam()` holds the settings; `BoundaryMergeParam(enabled = FALSE)`
stops at the first pass. `mergeCtwasBoundaryRegions()` is the same step for the
granular path:

```{r ctwas-merge, eval=FALSE}
merged <- mergeCtwasBoundaryRegions(
    finemapped,
    pipThresh = 0.5,
    filterCs = FALSE,
    maxSNP = Inf
)
```

## Common parameters

```{r ctwas-params, eval=FALSE}
ctwasPipeline(
    gwasSumStats = gwasByRegion,
    twasWeights = list(ctwasWeightsExample),
    method = NULL, # NULL: the TwasWeights' "ensemble" weights
    maxNumSingleEffects = 5,
    BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SerialParam(),
    keepSnps = FALSE,
    ctwasPriorParam = CtwasPriorParam(
        thin = 0.1,
        niterPrefit = 3,
        niter = 30,
        varStructure = "shared_nonSNP",
        fallbackToPrefit = FALSE
    ),
    variantPruningParam = VariantPruningParam(),
    boundaryMergeParam = BoundaryMergeParam()
)
```

With `method = NULL` a run uses the TwasWeights' pre-combined `"ensemble"`
weights. Weights without an ensemble, and a `QtlFineMappingResult` used as
the weight source, leave the choice open, so the pipeline asks for `method`.
Each run reads one method; compare methods by running each in turn.
